plain_english:
First, decide what kind of person you want to be. Then stick to that character whether you're alone or with others.

Stay quiet most of the time. When you do speak, say only what's necessary and keep it brief. You can join conversations occasionally when it makes sense, but don't let them drift into common topics like sports, celebrities, food, or drinks — the usual shallow stuff people talk about. And especially don't gossip about people — whether you're criticizing them, praising them, or comparing them. If you can steer the conversation toward better topics, do it. But if you're stuck with strangers, just stay quiet.

Don't laugh too loud, too often, or too much.
original_excerpt:
Begin by prescribing to yourself some character and demeanor, such as you may preserve both alone and in company.

Be mostly silent, or speak merely what is needful, and in few words. We may, however, enter sparingly into discourse sometimes, when occasion calls for it; but let it not run on any of the common subjects, as gladiators, or horse races, or athletic champions, or food, or drink—the vulgar topics of conversation—and especially not on men, so as either to blame, or praise, or make comparisons. If you are able, then, by your own conversation, bring over that of your company to proper subjects; but if you happen to find yourself among strangers, be silent.

Let not your laughter be loud, frequent, or abundant.

plain_english:
Don't make promises or swear oaths if you can help it. At least avoid them as much as possible.

Stay away from cheap, popular entertainment. But if you must go, stay alert. Don't let yourself slip into being crude without noticing. Remember this: even if you're a good person, spending time with corrupt people will corrupt you too.
original_excerpt:
Avoid taking oaths, if possible, altogether; at any rate, so far as you are able.

Avoid public and vulgar entertainments; but if ever an occasion calls you to them, keep your attention upon the stretch, that you may not imperceptibly slide into vulgarity. For be assured that if a person be ever so pure himself, yet, if his companion be corrupted, he who converses with him will be corrupted likewise.

plain_english:
Only give your body what it absolutely needs: food, water, clothes, shelter, basic help from others. Cut out anything that's just for show or luxury.

Before you get married, do everything you can to avoid sleeping with women. But don't be harsh or judgmental toward people who do this. And don't brag about how you're better than them.
original_excerpt:
Provide things relating to the body no further than absolute need requires, as meat, drink, clothing, house, retinue. But cut off everything that looks toward show and luxury.

Before marriage guard yourself with all your ability from unlawful intercourse with women; yet be not uncharitable or severe to those who are led into this, nor boast frequently that you yourself do otherwise.

plain_english: If someone tells you that a person spoke badly about you, don't defend yourself against what they said. Instead, respond: "He doesn't know about my other flaws, or he wouldn't have mentioned just those ones."
original_excerpt: If anyone tells you that a certain person speaks ill of you, do not make excuses about what is said of you, but answer: "He was ignorant of my other faults, else he would not have mentioned these alone."

plain_english: You don't need to go to public events very often. But when you do go, don't care more about anyone else than yourself. Want things to happen exactly as they do. Want the best person to win. This way, nothing will upset you. Don't cheer loudly, don't mock anyone, and don't get worked up. When you leave, don't spend a lot of time talking about what happened if it doesn't help you improve yourself. All that chatter just shows the spectacle impressed you too much.
original_excerpt: It is not necessary for you to appear often at public spectacles; but if ever there is a proper occasion for you to be there, do not appear more solicitous for any other than for yourself—that is, wish things to be only just as they are, and only the best man to win; for thus nothing will go against you. But abstain entirely from acclamations and derision and violent emotions. And when you come away, do not discourse a great deal on what has passed and what contributes nothing to your own amendment. For it would appear by such discourse that you were dazzled by the show.

plain_english:
Don't be eager to attend private readings and performances. But if you do go, stay serious and dignified. Just don't make yourself unpleasant.

When you're about to meet with someone — especially someone who seems above you — ask yourself how Socrates or Zeno would handle it. Then you'll know how to act, no matter what happens.
original_excerpt:
Be not prompt or ready to attend private recitations; but if you do attend, preserve your gravity and dignity, and yet avoid making yourself disagreeable.

When you are going to confer with anyone, and especially with one who seems your superior, represent to yourself how Socrates or Zeno would behave in such a case, and you will not be at a loss to meet properly whatever may occur.

plain_english: When you're going to meet someone in power, imagine ahead of time that they might not be home. You might be turned away. The doors might stay locked. They might ignore you completely. If you still have a duty to go, then go. Accept whatever happens. Never tell yourself afterward, "That wasn't worth the trouble." That kind of thinking is shallow. It shows you're confused about what really matters.
original_excerpt: When you are going before anyone in power, fancy to yourself that you may not find him at home, that you may be shut out, that the doors may not be opened to you, that he may not notice you. If, with all this, it be your duty to go, bear what happens and never say to yourself, "It was not worth so much"; for this is vulgar, and like a man bewildered by externals.

plain_english: When you're with other people, don't constantly talk about your own accomplishments and close calls. Sure, you might enjoy reliving your exciting moments, but others don't want to hear your war stories all the time. Also avoid trying too hard to make people laugh. This can easily make you look cheap, and it might make people respect you less. Stay away from dirty jokes and inappropriate conversations too. When someone starts going down that path, speak up and tell them to stop. Or at least show your disapproval by staying quiet, looking embarrassed, and keeping a serious expression.
original_excerpt: In company, avoid a frequent and excessive mention of your own actions and dangers. For however agreeable it may be to yourself to allude to the risks you have run, it is not equally agreeable to others to hear your adventures. Avoid likewise an endeavor to excite laughter, for this may readily slide you into vulgarity, and, besides, may be apt to lower you in the esteem of your acquaintance. Approaches to indecent discourse are likewise dangerous. Therefore, when anything of this sort happens, use the first fit opportunity to rebuke him who makes advances that way, or, at least, by silence and blushing and a serious look show yourself to be displeased by such talk.
